Americans have already staked more than $1.4 billion on prediction markets tied to the outcome of this year's U.S. midterm elections, and that figure is expected to exceed $2 billion by election day.

Millions of voters, alongside major trading firms and private companies, will trade on these markets—a boom that has provoked strong opposition from Democratic Party leaders, state governments, and much of the electorate.

"At issue are two questions: one of legality and one of prudence," writes @SamHenryLazarus in a new CFR report. "The first is whether election markets are legal to begin with—specifically, if they qualify as 'swaps' under federal commodities law and can therefore be offered nationwide. The second is whether the utility of election markets outweighs the risks they pose to the United States’ moral fabric, democratic process, and financial markets."

Election markets hold significant potential as tools for political forecasting, but only if policymakers take steps to control for insider trading and improve oversight, he argues.

Reform would serve both opponents and advocates of election markets, Lazarus argues. “Inaction will serve neither camp: scandals will abound, trust in the democratic process will erode, and traders will be defrauded.”

$PRME | FDA proposes adding new gene variants to an approved editing BLA without new clinical trials 🚨

On October 27, 2026, FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research issued a draft guidance, "Individualized Human Genome Editing Products: Considerations for BLA Submission and Postapproval Management".

It covers monogenic diseases where patients carry different pathogenic variants in the same gene. A single BLA under section 351(a) of the PHS Act can hold multiple product variants, each tailored to one mutation, bounded by a concept the guidance introduces: the individualized feature space, or IFS, the declared limits within which the editing components may vary.

Strength, formulation, the in vivo delivery vehicle such as the lipid nanoparticle, and the ex vivo cell type should remain constant across variants. What varies is typically the guide RNA. A variant falling inside the established IFS counts as a manufacturing change rather than a new product, submitted as a BLA supplement with in vitro activity data showing on-target editing at or above a clinically established threshold, plus NGS-based on-target and off-target safety data for each guide and editor combination. Where the link between in vitro data and clinical safety and effectiveness is well understood, FDA generally does not expect clinical data for those additions, and recommends an approved postapproval change management protocol under 21 CFR 601.12(e). Widening the IFS requires a prior approval supplement, and validation designed to cover the full IFS generally avoids revalidating per variant.

Prime Medicine's liver franchise is built on that architecture. The universal liver LNP holds formulation, GalNAc targeting ligand and prime editor mRNA constant and swaps only the guide RNAs, the same split FDA draws between fixed elements and variable features. PM577a targets ATP7B H1069Q, roughly 30 to 50 percent of Wilson disease alleles in the United States and Europe, with the first patient dosed in October 2026 and a follow-on R778L candidate in preclinical development. Those additional ATP7B variants could reach the label as supplements to the same application rather than as separate programs, sharply lowering the marginal cost of each additional mutation.

Three things set the ceiling. The IFS should be supported primarily by clinical data, and the applicant should justify that the variants actually studied span the entire proposed space, with extrapolation judged case by case on natural history, genotype-phenotype associations and genotype-driven safety factors, including variants producing no protein, where immunogenicity risk may rise. One studied variant supports a narrow space, not an open one. The framework also scales within a single gene and a single editing outcome, so the Wilson disease franchise and the SERPINA1 program behind PM647 would not share an IFS. And FDA's worked example varies a single guide RNA spacer, while a pegRNA varies across spacer, primer binding site and RT template, with a nicking guide alongside, so how wide a space that supports is unsettled.

The mechanism line falls where prime editing sits. Without naming it, FDA states that an editor relying on a reverse transcriptase does not belong in the same BLA as a base editor, since off-target and immunogenicity risks differ, and that adding one to an approved base editing product would be a new product requiring a new BLA. RT-based editing is treated as its own mechanistic class, which bounds what can later be folded into one application and equally keeps base editing BLAs from absorbing prime editors.

Wow, I'm really disappointed by this superficial and frankly unprofessional piece in @CJR.

There are many significant problems:

1. Calling frontier AI systems "autocomplete machines" is false and misleading. I don't know how we're still having this discussion in at the point where AI systems are routinely developing novel solutions to decades-old mathematical mysteries.

2. The claim that anthropomorphizing AI systems removes "accountability" or "acknowledgment" of flaws in the systems is also unsupported and provably false. Many people criticize Anthropic for "anthropomorphizing" Claude, but just read one of their system cards — they also acknowledge and take account of the systems' many flaws.

3. The piece recommends talking to the "experts," suggesting they all agree, but there is widespread disagreement among experts about how to characterize AI model behavior. Many, many experts do accept the "rogue" framing, e.g. https://t.co/WpfCr7ILHV
https://t.co/6mjnNuuDhK
https://t.co/2wedt2PTHx

Pretending that only the experts that agree with you exist is irresponsible journalism.

4. The piece's admonition not to "let anyone blow AI smoke up your ass" is unprofessional and also bad advice, as it doesn't provide any tools for actually assessing claims aside from knee-jerk skepticism. The piece claims that fears about catastrophic risk or the possibility of AI consciousness — again topics that many experts take seriously —  are just about building the companies' public image, but this is merely asserted without evidence.

5. When the piece gets around to trying to offer an argument for its thesis, that AI systems can't go rogue, it offers no actual evidence or reasoning. It doesn't engage with the facts of the Hugging Face hack or other related incidents. It just asserts that AI agent actions "shouldn't make the cut."

What's most baffling about all this is these are very controversial claims, not only among AI experts but with journalism. Many highly credible news outlets have embraced the "rogue" characterization. It's possible they're making a mistake, but this piece offers no actual reason to think so.
